story:
Idris was the second prophet after Adam, described in the Quran as trustworthy and patient, and said to have been "exalted to a high station." He was born in Babylon. Before receiving divine revelation, he followed the teachings that had been given to Seth, the son of Adam. When he grew older, God made him a prophet. At that time the people did not follow God's message and instead worshipped fire. Idris urged his people to abandon their wrongdoing, but many refused to listen, so he left Babylon; some of his people, though reluctant to leave their home, went with him. They asked him where they would find a place as good as Babylon; he told them that if they migrated for God's sake, God would provide for them. They traveled to Egypt and saw the Nile River, where Idris stood on its bank and glorified God.

Idris divided his time: three days a week he preached to his people, and four days he devoted entirely to worship. He was among the first men to write with a pen, the first to observe the movement of the stars, and he set out weights and measures. He was also credited with inventing the art of making garments.

Concerning his being raised to a high station: God told Idris that he would credit him daily with the good deeds of all of Adam's descendants. Wanting to increase his own good deeds further, Idris asked a friend among the angels to help him speak with the angel of death. This angel carried Idris on its wings up through the heavens. In the fourth heaven they met the angel of death, who was descending toward the earth to take Idris's soul. Astonished, the angel of death took Idris's soul there in the fourth heaven, fulfilling the words that he was raised to a high station.

During Muhammad's Night Journey through the heavens, he encountered Idris in the fourth heaven.
blind:
The prophet was the second holy messenger after the first man. He was described as trustworthy and patient, and said to have been raised to a high station. He was born in a great city. Before receiving revelation, he followed the teachings passed down from an earlier holy man, the son of the first man. When he grew older, the deity made him a prophet. At that time, the people did not follow the deity's message and instead worshipped fire. The prophet urged his people to give up their wrongdoing, but many refused, so he left the city; some of his people, though reluctant, went with him. They asked him where they would find a place like their home city; he told them that if they migrated for the sake of the deity, the deity would provide for them. They traveled to a foreign land and saw a great river, where the prophet stood at its bank and glorified the deity.

The prophet divided his time: three days a week preaching to his people, four days devoted entirely to worship. He was among the first to use a writing instrument, the first to observe the movement of the stars, and he established measures and weights. He was also credited with inventing the art of making garments.

Concerning his being raised to a high station: the deity told the prophet that he would credit him daily with the good deeds of all descendants of the first man. Wanting to increase his own good deeds, the prophet asked a friend among the heavenly messengers to help him speak with the angel who takes souls. This heavenly being carried him on its wings up through the heavens. In the fourth heaven they met the angel who takes souls, who was descending toward the earth to take the prophet's soul. Astonished, the angel took the prophet's soul then and there, in the fourth heaven, fulfilling the words that he was raised to a high station.

During another holy messenger's night journey through the heavens, that messenger encountered the prophet in the fourth heaven.
